en: These chapters follow that path without repeating the original numbering. The techno-economic order is covered in the chapters on technique and on how the platform extracts value, and the semiotic dimension and private power in the chapters on the law of the platform, semiotic vulnerability, and information, advertising and anticipation. The regime and the control concepts come next, from the chapter on the object to the one on protected legal interests, and the integrated reading of the Constitution, the CDC and intellectual property appears in the chapters on the constitutional order, intellectual property and proof. The applications are found in the platform pages and in the chapter on remedies.

The third section reconstructs the techno-economic order of platforms, describing how technical rationality and models of continuous extraction reorganize the conditions of possibility of contemporary digital consumption. The fourth section examines the semiotic and subjective dimension of immaterial consumption, making explicit the means through which signs, belonging, rhythm and performance modulate expectations and conduct, thus intensifying asymmetries relevant to consumer protection.<1>p. 42</1>

In the fifth section, the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption is consolidated as an infrastructure-concept, and operational control concepts are set out that are apt to guide the identification and qualification of abusive practices in continuous digital environments, with emphasis on semiotic vulnerability, abusive teleology as a controllable category of attribution, and parameters such as open auditability and functional value equivalence.<1>p. 42</1>

The sixth section carries out the dogmatic reconstruction, proposing an integrated reading of the 1988 Federal Constitution of the Federative Republic of Brazil, the Consumer Protection Code, and Brazilian legislation on intellectual property rights from the standpoint of the IOC regime, so as to make explicit criteria of legal qualification, correlated duties and possible institutional responses to conflicts on digital consumption platforms.<1>p. 42</1>

The seventh section brings together illustrative applications and tests of fit for the proposed keys in typical contemporary situations of continuous digital consumption, using examples and public documentary material to make visible recurring patterns of friction, evidentiary demands and blind spots in the translation of the conflict, without turning the work into an extended case study.<1>p. 42</1>

The dogmatic chapters lead into parameters, and using them calls for three distinctions. The parameter is the criterion that organizes the reading of the case, an operational statement that does not replace legal reasoning with a ready-made formula. The normative basis is the legal rule on which the qualification rests, such as the immaterial product of Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>. The consequence is what can be requested, the possible institutional consequence, which should favor restoration of access, reversal of sanctions, preservation of history and equivalent functional substitution, with monetary compensation as a residual or complementary response.

The parameters synthesized at the end of the preceding dogmatic reconstruction then take on a properly operative function. They no longer present themselves as mere moments of theoretical elaboration, but as references applicable to the institutional reading of the conflict.<1>pp. 714-715</1>

It is at this point that the parameters take the form of operational statements, which do not replace legal reasoning with ready-made formulas, but prevent the incidence of the IOC from depending, at each new conflict, on an exhaustive return to the reconstructive itinerary that grounded their elaboration.<1>p. 716</1>

The possible legal qualification varies according to the main incidence of the case, but the institutional consequence should favor restoration of access, reversal of sanctions, preservation of history, equivalent functional substitution, governance adjustments, injunctive relief and structural correction when the harm reveals a repeatable pattern. Monetization remains possible, but as a residual or complementary response, not as an automatic reflex of the injury.<1>p. 748</1>

Application follows a repeatable sequence, from the governance mechanism and the friction it produces to the vulnerability triggered, the compatible standard of proof and the possible consequence. The criteria work with possible proof and controllable inferences, without requiring full access to algorithms and internal records. The table of situations, which remains for reference, does not aim to mechanize the decision, and it organizes the passage between governance structure, breached duty, minimum proof, legal qualification and possible consequence.

The application of these parameters is guided by a repeatable sequence. One starts from the predominant governance mechanism and the type of friction it produces. The central vulnerability triggered in the relationship is identified. The standard of proof compatible with the structure of the conflict is set. Finally, the possible dogmatic consequence under the IOC regime is indicated.<1>p. 715</1>

Criteria of incidence cannot depend on full access to algorithms, logs and internal rules as a condition of possibility, since that would turn the IOC into an impracticable category, reserved for exceptional cases.<1>p. 429</1>

For the IOC, the criteria must operate with possible proof and controllable inferences, capable of stabilizing expectations about the core of the enjoyment bundle even when the ecosystem tries to naturalize opacity and reconfigurability as if they were indisputable facts.<1>p. 429</1>

This table does not aim to mechanize the decision or to reduce the complexity of the environment to a rigid formula. Its function is more honest and more useful. It organizes, in consultable language, the passage between governance structure, breached duty, minimum evidentiary demand, legal qualification and possible institutional consequence.<1>p. 748</1>
What if they say it's just a game?

The first objection is that it is just a game. That laughter or disdain is part of the problem, because social disdain makes the injury easier, more acceptable and more invisible. Gaming platforms move significant sums in microtransactions, virtual goods and competitive events, while the legal system still operates, to a large extent, with categories designed for tangible goods and one-off performances.

When the activity of an entire economic sector is treated as harmless play, it becomes easier for abuses to be examined from the perspective of “it’s just a game”, even when they involve money, time, attention, legitimate expectations and relevant losses.<1>p. 22</1>

There is, however, a predictable social reflex whenever one mentions the aim of treating interactive entertainment as a technical, market, existential and patrimonial category. The reaction is at times laughter, puzzlement or disdain. This reflex is part of the very problem the thesis confronts, because social disdain is one of the mechanisms that makes the injury easier, more acceptable and more invisible.<1>p. 22</1>

Online gaming platforms have ceased to be peripheral spaces of youth leisure and have become environments in which significant sums circulate around microtransactions, virtual goods, targeted advertising and the organization of competitive events of global reach. In this scenario, Brazil presents itself simultaneously as a large consumer market and as a legal system that still operates, to a large extent, with categories designed for an analog world, based on tangible goods and one-off performances, even if repeated.<1>p. 37</1>

The second is that the exclusivity of intellectual property would authorize free management of the experience. But the protection of immaterial creations is no license for the arbitrary management of consumption, and the IOC regime does not aim to annul exclusivities, only to locate the point of tension, because exploiting the sign and access does not eliminate minimum duties of stability, verifiable transparency and restoration.

Exclusivity may organize the market, but it cannot justify an environment in which the consumer bears systematic losses without an intelligible language of justification, without traceability and without conditions for challenge.<1>p. 25</1>
The legal protection of immaterial creations, however, does not operate as a license for the arbitrary management of consumption experiences.<1>p. 25</1>

In this sense, the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption does not oppose intellectual property as if it were a project to annul exclusivities. It fixes the point of institutional tension. Under continuous consumption, the economic exploitation of the sign and of access does not eliminate minimum duties of stability, verifiable transparency and restoration when there is relevant degradation of enjoyment.<1>p. 25</1>

The third is that the sector's repeated practice would count as custom. On the platform, however, repetition is not a sufficient sign of legitimacy, because market habit is often already the product of unilateral design and of choices filtered by the architecture. The fourth is that a researcher familiar with the ecosystem would be biased, and the answer lies in the method, in which the position in the field is a sensitivity for detecting hypotheses, always confronted with institutional documentation and traceable records.

The researcher's position in the field does not operate as a criterion of proof, but as a sensitivity for detecting reading hypotheses, which remain subject to confrontation with institutional documentation and traceable records, so as to prevent frictions and controversies from being treated as anecdote.<1>p. 79</1>
What does this doctrine not claim?

The limits are declared from the outset. There is no microsystem, no exhaustive empirical demonstration and no systematic survey, and the applications are illustrative. The mere fact of governing is not abusive teleology, and the evolution of the service does not become unlawful in itself. There is no intent to open avenues of accusation against the subjects cited, and the aims are theoretical and dogmatic. No chapter, therefore, concludes that a company or a practice is abusive, and what is offered are categories and criteria for demonstrating and requesting, depending on the case. In the writing and revision of the underlying research, artificial intelligence systems supported the organization of the text, the comparison of formulations and the detection of inconsistencies, without replacing the research or altering the criterion of proof.

Public documentary materials and institutional sources are used for the purpose of anchoring and exemplifying the dogmatic path, without constituting an exhaustive empirical corpus. This choice stems from the object itself, since the axis of the work is the dogmatic reconstruction of categories of qualification, proof and attribution applicable to continuous digital consumption, and not the production of generalizations by sampling.<1>p. 40</1>

In operational terms, the aim is to select and analyze, for illustrative purposes and for their dogmatic pertinence, public statements by consumers related to the League of Legends ecosystem, as well as to examine terms of use, policies and interface mechanisms relevant to the governance of the service. From this public documentary material and typical examples, the aim is to make explicit how practices of hypercuratorial anticipation, curation and sanction interact with the legal regime of the IOC, so as to make recurring patterns of friction adjudicable without shifting the argument toward a claim of systematic survey.<1>p. 39</1>

Moreover, it should be clarified that the text of this research carries no intent to establish avenues of accusation regarding any subjects cited or analyzed. The proposal has strictly scientific objectives of a theoretical-dogmatic order, aimed at building categories and criteria for interpreting the law in force for the pacification of conflicts in consumer relations marked by structural asymmetry, seeking solely the promotion of techniques apt to restore material balance and the controllability of performances in continuous digital environments.<1>p. 42</1>

Consistent with this discipline of methodological transparency, it is also recorded that, throughout the writing and revision, artificial intelligence systems were used as support tools for textual organization, the comparison of formulations and the detection of argumentative inconsistencies. The use of these tools does not replace the research, does not alter the criterion of proof and produces no interpretive authority.<1>p. 80</1>

How the platform extracts value

Platform consumption tends to be organized around a business model that extracts value from control of access, from manufactured scarcity and from the consumer's own presence, and this model explains supplier conduct that reading a clause in isolation cannot reach. Read with Varoufakis, Dowbor and Marx, the model gives the jurist conditions of attribution, and not a condemnation of the market.
Why does a consumer lawyer need to read the business model?

The political economy of platform consumption begins with risk. The company needs to govern the contingencies of the business, and this governance tends to operate by displacement, shifting part of the risk and the social cost onto third parties and the State. Internal risks, such as the production chain, logistics and quality, as a rule stay under the company's management, while external ones reach the consumer's health, property, privacy, lifetime and informational environment. Risk never reaches zero, and the problem begins when the company lowers its own risk by spreading the effects over consumers, society and the State.

The decisive point is that this governance of risks rarely remains confined to the organization. It tends to operate through mechanisms of displacement, transferring relevant portions of risk and social cost to third parties and to the State, which is often called upon only afterward to restore the broken balance.<1>p. 139</1>

Internal risks are those that bear directly on the performance of the enterprise: production chain, logistics, quality standards, reputation and organizational capacity. As a rule, they remain manageable by the company, since they depend on governance, compliance, investment in quality and operational control. External risks, although they may be triggered by economic activity, manifest themselves more diffusely and outside the supplier's immediate sphere of control. They reach the health, integrity, property, privacy, lifetime and informational environment of consumers, as well as competitors, communities and institutional ecosystems.<1>p. 140</1>

It is in the domain of external risks that the paradoxical dimension of the “perfect business” becomes evident: an operation capable of maximizing gains while keeping under control, at least from the business point of view, the risks that threaten its own stability. This threshold can never be reduced to zero, as consumer-law quality theory recognizes when it admits the inevitability of failures and the need for preventive and remedial discipline of supply. The problem begins when the internal minimization of risk is achieved by the diffuse transfer of its effects to consumers, society and the State.<1>p. 140</1>

This is where Consumer Law comes in. The company also profits by designing structures that organize responsibilities and distribute burdens, and, if profit depends on allocating risks, the discipline that sets minimum standards of adequacy and safety works as a legal containment of the tendency to externalize them. In the classic paradigm, the food industrialist must ensure that the product matches what it promises and causes no harm over time, and the State must set minimum parameters and hold accountable those who violate them.

The supplier is liable because it occupies the structural position of the one who reaps the gains of the activity and, therefore, must internalize preventively and, when necessary, through effective reparation, the cost of the risks it creates.<1>p. 140</1>

The company does not maximize results merely by producing more or selling better; it maximizes results by designing structures that organize responsibilities, filter obligations and distribute burdens. Profit therefore depends on risk allocation strategies.<1>p. 140</1>
By establishing minimum standards of adequacy and safety, Consumer Law works as a legal containment of the tendency toward externalization.<1>p. 140</1>

The industrialist who exploits the food market must ensure, as a condition of the business's viability, that its product at least minimally matches what it promises. Adequacy is not limited to immediate performance, such as taste, shelf life or appearance; it includes safety and quality over time, so that the product does not harm the physical, psychological or patrimonial integrity of the consumer. At this point, the State not only may intervene: it must set minimum parameters and hold the supplier accountable when they are violated.<1>p. 140</1>

On platforms, the place of risk changes. In the industrial paradigm the inspection of risk can fall on the composition, performance and safety of the product, while in the techno-media order it shifts to the conditions of access, the governance regimes, the decision architectures and the semiotic layer of the promise. Externalization comes to operate through informational asymmetry, opaque criteria, lack of auditability and loss of control over one's own experience, and the platform, at once the place of the offer and the place where the conditions of enjoyment are managed, heightens the possibility of shifting burdens onto the consumer.

In the classic industrial paradigm, the social and legal inspection of risk can fall on the materiality of the product, such as composition, performance and safety. In the techno-media order, risk tends to shift to conditions of access, governance regimes, decision architectures and to the semiotic layer that sustains the promise of consumption.<1>p. 141</1>

In environments organized by technical layers and interface languages, externalization tends to operate through indirect and diffuse routes, in the form of informational asymmetry, opacity of criteria, absence of auditability and loss of control over one's own consumption experience.<1>p. 141</1>

The platform becomes simultaneously the place of the offer and the place where the conditions of enjoyment are managed. With this, the possibility of shifting burdens onto the consumer and onto the public sphere intensifies.<1>p. 142</1>

That is why political economy enters as a condition of attribution. If power comes from control of infrastructure and the capacity to charge tolls, the injury need not appear as a one-off defect or explicit nonperformance, and it may consist in the relevant and unilateral degradation of the enjoyment bundle, in costs of staying, in reduced visibility, in the modulation of access or in the reconfiguration of internal equivalences. The object may go on existing for accounting purposes while the supplier reconfigures the architecture that gave it utility, distinction or recognition, and the gaming scenario is not an anomaly of entertainment but a general form of economic organization through infrastructure.
On platforms, the formal permanence of the item in the account does not guarantee the preservation of its functional, symbolic or economic value.<1>p. 145</1>

In this framework, political economy does not enter as an external diagnosis, but as a condition of attribution. If economic power derives from control of infrastructure and the capacity to impose tolls, the injury in consumption need not appear only as a one-off defect or explicit nonperformance. It may consist in the relevant and unilateral degradation of the enjoyment bundle, in the imposition of costs of staying, in the reduction of visibility, in the modulation of access or in the reconfiguration of internal equivalences.<1>p. 152</1>
The object may continue “existing” for accounting and contractual purposes, while the architecture that gave it utility, distinction or recognition is reconfigured by the supplier.<1>p. 145</1>
The decisive point is that the illustrative scenario does not describe a sectoral anomaly of entertainment, but a general form of economic organization through infrastructure.<1>p. 145</1>
What does Varoufakis describe as technofeudalism?

Yanis Varoufakis supplies the macro level. In his account, capital comes to be concentrated in the cloud, in digital assets, platforms and algorithms resting on a physical base of data warehouses, servers and cables, and this capital is the power to control channels of access, circulation, data, visibility and transaction. It reproduces itself without proportional extra costs for its holders, the cloudalists, a rendering of the term nubelistas from the Spanish edition, and the platform stops being an intermediary and functions as private territory, in which users, suppliers and creators depend on internal rules to exist economically.

The author argues that the capitalist system would be on the way to being replaced by what he calls “technofeudalism”, in which capital ceases to present itself primarily as material property and comes to be concentrated “in the cloud”, that is, in digital assets, online platforms and algorithms. The critique deserves recognition for highlighting that this cloud capital, held by those he categorizes as “cloudalists” (in our translation from “nubelistas”, from the Spanish edition), has as its characteristic the capacity to reproduce itself without generating proportional extra costs for its owners.<1>p. 142</1>

Cloud capital requires, on the one hand, a planetary physical infrastructure, composed of data warehouses, servers, sensors and cables, which makes possible the continuous capture and processing of interactions.<1>p. 157</1>

“Cloud capital” does not designate only computational infrastructure, but a form of economic power capable of controlling channels of access, circulation, data, visibility and transaction. The platform ceases to act as a mere intermediary between market agents and comes to function as private territory in which users, consumers, suppliers and creators depend on internal rules to exist economically.<1>p. 146</1>

For Varoufakis, the criterion that defines the new system is the replacement of profit by rent. Profit tends to be eroded by competition, whereas rent rests on a position of control, which is why he speaks of rupture rather than of an advanced phase of capitalism, with markets giving way to platforms that function as fiefdoms. The cloudalists are the new lords, the population becomes cloud serfs or cloud proletariat, depending on the degree of dependence, and producers who can sell only through access to someone else's digital territory are vassal capitalists. Profit does not disappear as an ambition, but it loses its place as the central fuel of accumulation.

Profit tends to be eroded by competition, while rent is sustained by a position of control and therefore resists competitive dynamics in a different way <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 106-107)</2>.<3>p. 149</3>

Varoufakis explicitly maintains that technofeudalism should not be understood as an "advanced phase" of capitalism, but as a structural rupture, in which capitalist dynamics would cease to govern contemporary economies and would be replaced by a distinct system.<1>p. 147</1>
In parallel, the population at large is converted into cloud serfs and cloud proletariat, according to the degree of dependence and capture of the activity.<1>p. 153</1>

The image does not function merely as a descriptive device. It is formalized, in the conceptual apparatus of technofeudalism, by the figure of the vassal capitalists, producers who remain capitalists at the level of production, but whose possibility of selling comes to depend on access to proprietary digital territories.<1>p. 161</1>

Even so, Varoufakis preserves a relevant nuance. Profit does not disappear as an ambition of economic agents and as a cultural horizon of advancement, but its systemic status is altered, since accumulation can become dissociated from profit as its central fuel and shift the focus to the recurring extraction associated with the access regime.<1>p. 163</1>

What matters most to the jurist is the demand monopoly, which for Varoufakis is not a monopoly of supply but the capacity to capture and govern the path to the consumer, so that power comes to manage the very possibility of choice. In his view, even the worst markets preserve some horizontal interaction among buyers, who exchange information and even organize boycotts, while algorithmic mediation isolates demand and steers it along internal tracks. The pressure point he identifies is interoperability, the possibility of migrating between platforms without losing data, histories and collections, which moves the regulatory target from price and size to the design of access and portability.
Freedom of choice, therefore, does not disappear as an abstract possibility, but becomes more expensive as a practice.<1>p. 175</1>

Especially relevant to the central discussion of this work is the concept of demand monopoly addressed by Varoufakis <1>(2024)</1>, because it names a form of power that is not reduced to the monopoly “of supply”, nor to the formal exclusivity typical of classic competition law, consisting, rather, in the capacity to capture and govern the path to the consumer.<2>p. 173</2>

The decisive point is that, by replacing markets with fiefdoms in the cloud, power is not limited to charging more, as a classic monopolist would, since it comes to manage the very possibility of choice, that is, the form and conditions under which buyers and sellers meet. That is why Varoufakis insists that even the worst markets still preserve some degree of horizontal interaction (buyers can exchange information, form associations and even organize boycotts) whereas, in the world of the platform, algorithmic mediation blocks this common space and suppresses minimum counterweights, isolating demand and guiding it along internal tracks.<1>p. 174</1>

Even so, Varoufakis identifies a point of regulatory pressure that the lords of the cloud would genuinely fear. It is interoperability, understood as the user's ability to migrate between fiefdoms without losing data, histories and collections, that is, without paying the exit cost that sustains dependence. Here, the target ceases to be “price” or “size” and becomes the design of access and portability, that is, the mechanism that turns infrastructure into recurring rent.<1>p. 169-170</1>

The diagnosis reaches consumption through the player who buys cosmetics and whose enjoyment is affected by reworks, which are redesigns of an item or character made by the supplier. The consumer keeps formal ownership of what is in the account, but the skin functions as a conditional permission to enjoy within a private domain, and not as a fully alienated commodity. Revenue that looks like profit from sales behaves as rent from control, and banning and graduated sanctions operate as functional expropriation, because they force the consumer to rebuild reputation and access with new investment. In this reading, the IOC is the legal-descriptive form for grasping in consumption what technofeudalism describes at the macro scale.

The scenario of the player who acquires cosmetics and has their enjoyment affected by reworks makes it possible to visualize, in miniature, what Varoufakis describes at the macro scale. The platform operates as a landlord of infrastructure: it controls the environment, the rules, the updates and the visibility of what acquires value there. “Cloud capital” appears as dominion over access, reputation and permanence, so that the consumer, although keeping formal ownership of items linked to the account, remains subject to the unilateral power to modulate utility, prestige and conditions of enjoyment.<1>p. 146</1>

The point becomes clearer when one observes that a skin and its associated content do not operate as a fully alienated commodity, but as a conditioned permission of enjoyment within a private domain. The platform may preserve the nominal existence of the item in the account and, even so, downgrade its enjoyment bundle by altering its appearance, its effects, its insertion in the internal economy or its criteria of social display. In this dynamic, revenue that looks like “profit from sales” behaves as rent from control, since the platform captures value by managing access and by governing the scarcity, visibility and practical equivalence of what is enjoyed. The same pattern reappears in banning and graduated sanctions, which function as forms of functional expropriation and as mechanisms of economic recapture, because they force the consumer to rebuild, through new investment of time, attention and property, their reputation, their access and their signs of belonging within the same managed territory.<1>p. 149-150</1>
The IOC, in this sense, is the legal-descriptive form for grasping, at the level of consumption, what technofeudalism describes at the macro level.<1>p. 152</1>
Where does Dowbor diverge from Varoufakis, and why does it matter?

Ladislau Dowbor offers the intermediate level. In his account, a rentier capitalism is taking hold, in which power lies in owning and controlling assets, and not in producing goods. Platforms are demand monopolies because one must use what others use in order to communicate, and rent comes from the toll economy, in which rentiers earn less from the services they provide than from everyone being obliged to pass through their turnstiles. As he sums it up, today one owns a process and charges for its use.
Dowbor identifies rentier capitalism as a system in which power lies in the possession and control of assets, rather than in the production of goods.<1>p. 142</1>

“The result is the so-called ‘demand monopolies’: we have to use what others use, because without it we do not communicate, besides the fact that they buy any competitor that tries to open space” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 24)</2>.<3>p. 184-185</3>

“Many services are useful, or even necessary, but generate profits disproportionate to the contribution, as in the case of communication oligopolies. Rentiers earn not so much from the services they provide as from everyone's obligation to pass through their turnstiles.” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 21)</2>.<3>p. 185</3>

The change is profound because it marks the passage from an era of producers and buyers to an era of suppliers and users <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51)</2>, in which the central economic mechanism ceases to be the good and becomes the process. In this sense, today one owns a process and charges for its use <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 52)</4>.<5>p. 200</5>

Dowbor's most useful contribution for the lawyer is the move from cost to proof. Monetization works through micro-drainage, a fractional and repeated extraction, and the platform alone controls the logs, which are the system's automatic records, the metrics and the criteria for profiling, ranking and recommendation, while the consumer sees only the interface. The problem comes to involve proof and material transparency, and the relevant harm may occur before any financial loss, in the intelligibility of the offer and in the formation of the decision.

“Micro-drainage” designates a fractional and repeated extraction, made possible by algorithmic capillarity and by inference technologies that make each individual addressable as an economic target, and operationalized by tracking devices such as cookies and related identifiers.<1>p. 190</1>

The platform centralizes and exclusively controls logs, metrics and modulation criteria, such as profiling, ranking and recommendation, while the consumer sees only the interface and its effects. As a result, the problem ceases to be only one of “cost” and comes to involve proof and material transparency, since the user has no means to reconstruct the link between capture, processing and consequences in the offer and the experience.<1>p. 190</1>

Since this capture takes place through governance, through interested curation, segmentation and persuasive interface architecture, consumer protection cannot be reduced to subsequent patrimonial restoration. The relevant harm may occur earlier, in the intelligibility of the offer and in the very shaping of the decision.<1>p. 192</1>

The two authors do not agree, however, on what to call the system. Varoufakis expressly rejects names that imply continuity, such as hypercapitalism and rentier capitalism, because they would hide the return of rent to the center, and rentier capitalism is precisely Dowbor's label. The two work as lenses on the same reality at different levels, and with Dowbor the figure of the technofief gains a sharper economic definition as a passage to platform capitalism, but reading them together does not erase the divergence. The prudent course is to credit each with what is his, the fief, the serfs and cloud rent to Varoufakis, the toll, the turnstiles and the owner of a process to Dowbor, and to rest the legal argument on the point where the two converge, the conversion of access into rent.

In terms of the architecture of economic power, the argument gains density by asserting that the "pillars" of capitalism are in fact replaced by pillars proper to technofeudalism, articulating "cloud fiefs" and "cloud rent" as the explanatory core of a mode of accumulation and domination that reconfigures the forms of dependence and access <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 9)</2>. Within this frame, Varoufakis <3>(2024, p. 115)</3> expressly rejects the nomenclatures of continuity (such as “hypercapitalism” or “rentier capitalism”) because, in his view, they obscure the defining trait of the present, marked by the recentralization of rent and by the transformation of the market into territory managed by proprietary infrastructures.<4>p. 148</4>

At the macro level, Varoufakis describes platforms operating as cloud technofiefs. At the meso level, Dowbor emphasizes digital rentierism and the toll economy. At the micro level, Marx provides the key to perceiving how digital consumption can function as the invisible labor of a contemporary kind of “informational lumpenproletariat”.<1>p. 143</1>

With the macroeconomic perspective of the technofeudal system established, the next step is to show how the same reality is expressed, through another theoretical lens, as an economy of rentierism and demand monopoly. In Dowbor, the core is not the cloud as fief, but the control of informational and financial circuits capable of imposing recurring extractions, not as market price, but as systematic rent.<1>p. 183</1>

The figure of the technofief reaches, with Dowbor, a sharper economic determination by situating the passage from industrial capitalism to a platform capitalism marked by digital rentierism.<1>p. 195</1>

Within the scope adopted here, Dowbor's critique matters above all for the way the platform converts access into rent through control of informational flows and of decisions on visibility, access and permanence.<1>p. 188</1>
What do a game's terms say about the account, the currency and the collection?

The Riot Games Terms of Service set out in their clauses the structure Varoufakis describes, and there the feudal grammar begins to operate as the language of the relationship. The terms say that virtual content is a personal right, that the user has no ownership of the account and that all rights to it are and always will be the company's, without distinguishing those who spent years accumulating signs of belonging from those who have just arrived.

The argument gains empirical density when one descends from the macro level to the letter of the platform contract, where the feudal grammar ceases to be a theoretical figure and comes to operate as the operative language of the relationship.<1>p. 153</1>

Riot states that virtual content is a “personal right” and that there is no user ownership of the account, and also records that “all rights” to this account “will always be” Riot's <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 154</3>

The contract does not distinguish those who spent years accumulating signs of belonging from those who have just arrived, because what is at stake is not the merit of the effort or the expenditure of resources on cosmetic items, but the platform's ownership structure.<1>p. 153</1>

Termination follows the same logic. The account may be terminated or suspended on what the company calls a reasonable determination, including for what it describes as the best interest of the community or the services, and the user then loses the account, the associated data and the virtual content, in-game currency included, without refund whenever the company considers there was cause. An official support document admits that negative behavior may result in a permanent ban at any time and without prior warning. A threat need not be carried out in order to govern, since it is enough that it be credible.

What is bought, in practice, is a tolerance of access that can be withdrawn, and the withdrawal need not justify itself according to an external theory of legitimacy, because it is self-sufficient in the internal language of the lordship.<1>p. 153</1>

Riot provides for termination and suspension based on what it calls a “reasonable” determination, and lists cases that include violation, but also what it itself describes as the “best interest” of the community or of its services <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 154</3>

Once the account is terminated, the user will no longer have access to the account, nor to the associated data, nor to the Virtual Content, including in-game currency, and the consequence is definitive loss without refund when the lord considers there was cause <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 155</3>

In an official League of Legends support document, the language is even more direct in admitting that negative behavior “may result in a permanent ban at any time” and “without prior warnings or suspensions” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2026e)</2>.<3>p. 155</3>
The threat need not be applied in order to govern. It needs to be credible.<1>p. 155</1>

The clauses on currency complete the picture. The company admits that it may sometimes increase the number of coins needed to buy skins, and that it may adjust prices with future effect, except for what has already been acquired. The terms deny any value to the virtual content of the account, and this denial is functional, because it makes internal inflation and lost purchasing power look like natural variation rather than the erosion of the consumer's economic position. Capping liability at the amounts paid in the previous twelve months, and excluding indirect damages except where that would be illegal, is a calculation that ignores prolonged accumulation, dependence and exit cost. The clauses' own caveats, however, need to be read in full.

Riot admits that “sometimes” it may “change the purchasing power of the Game Currency” and spells out the mechanism: “we may increase the number of Game Currency needed to buy Virtual Products, such as skins” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. At the same time, it states that “we may adjust the prices of any part of the Riot Services at any time (with future effect, that is, with the exception of what you have already acquired)” and that it may “modify, change or supplement our pricing and billing methods with future effect”, effective “immediately upon posting” <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2024e)</4>.<5>p. 176</5>

The contract expressly denies any value attributed to data residing on servers operated or controlled by Riot, including Game Content and Virtual Content associated with the account. The denial is not symbolic. It is functional. If the collection is legally described as having no value, internal inflation and the loss of purchasing power come to be treated as natural variation of the fief, not as deterioration of an economic position relevant to the consumer <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 176-177</3>

The limitation clause provides that total liability may be limited to the amounts paid by the user in the 12 months prior to the cause arising, and also excludes unforeseeable losses and indirect damages, except to the extent that it would be illegal to do so <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 177</3>

The platform reserves the power to govern value, currency and access within the territory, but tries to lower the civil response for losses to a calculation that ignores precisely what makes the fief efficient, which is prolonged accumulation, dependence and exit cost.<1>p. 177</1>

The strong vocabulary of this analysis, such as legal humiliation and civilized blackmail, draws its cruelty from the written mechanism of expropriation, and not from moral discourse about behavior, and the word bribe, applied to symbolic rewards, is meant metaphorically. In a court filing, these expressions serve to describe the mechanism, and not to characterize the conduct.
The figure of the cloudalist, when it crosses the rhetoric and enters the letter of the contract, reveals a point of legal humiliation that is structural to technofeudalism.<1>p. 153</1>
Cloud rent appears here in the form of civilized blackmail.<1>p. 154</1>
When the technofeudal thesis calls for a moment of cruelty, it does not come from moral discourse about behavior. It comes from the written mechanism of expropriation.<1>p. 154</1>

Here, the word “bribe” is used metaphorically to describe how consumer loyalty is captured through a "symbolic sustenance", in which the supplier trades mere lines of code and calibrated scarcity for hours of the user's life and attention.<1>p. 224</1>

The lawyer takes something else from the case. The contract is not a pathological exception but the legal form in which the structure puts itself in writing, and the denial of value it contains does not decide whether the loss is legally relevant, because it tries to collapse by definition what in practice functions as accumulated immaterial assets. Under the CDC, the problem translates into the factual vulnerability of Article 4, item I, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>, which justifies heightened duties of transparency, loyalty and information.

The contract observed is not a pathological exception. It is the legal form in which the technofeudal structure states itself in writing, and therefore it makes it possible to recognize, at the macro level, the same institutional design that organizes the ecosystem.<1>p. 155</1>
The clause is relevant because it tries to collapse, by definition, what in practice operates as accumulated immaterial assets.<1>p. 177</1>

It is this passage that makes it possible to translate, in dogmatic terms, the vulnerability intrinsic to immaterial objects of consumption as an interpreted dimension of the factual vulnerability of Article 4, item I, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>, justifying reinforced duties of transparency, loyalty and information.<3>p. 183</3>
How does what is abundant become scarce?

The next question is how value is extracted from goods that are not scarce. Dowbor recalls that shared knowledge is not lost to those who share it, because it is not a rival good, and from there the conflict shifts to the control of access. If reproduction is cheap, a persistent regime of unavailability, exclusivity and last chance does not reveal a natural condition of the object, but an institutional choice, and scarcity appears as a project, sustained by enclosures in which intellectual property, licenses, account architecture and access control become governance infrastructure.

When technical reproduction is cheap and availability could be expanded, rent is not sustained by natural rarity, but by produced rarefaction, which shifts the center of gravity of economic power.<1>p. 208</1>

In the informational paradigm, knowledge takes the position of central factor of production, but its economic logic is not the same as that of physical goods, since, unlike material goods, shared knowledge is not lost to those who share it, as it is not a rival good and access to it can be generalized <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 11)</2>. This non-rivalry shifts the axis of the conflict to the forms of access control, which makes intelligible why immaterial consumer goods and digital experiences, as IOCs, may be technically reproducible and, even so, legally and technically made scarce through regimes of authorization and blocking that organize consumption.<3>p. 188</3>

In digital objects, the marginal cost of reproduction tends to fall drastically and, in theory, availability could expand without requiring productive capacity comparable to the factory, logistics and the extraction of inputs. Therefore, when a persistent regime of unavailability, exclusivity and last chance is observed in these markets, one is not facing a natural condition of the object, but a deliberate institutional choice, so that scarcity appears not as a fact, but as a project.<1>p. 209</1>

In the informational environment, the toll economy is realized with special effectiveness through legal-technical enclosures, since intellectual property rights, license contracts, account architecture and access control mechanisms become governance infrastructure and turn access to and permanence in the ecosystem into a recurring source of extraction <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 7; p. 21; p. 41)</2>.<3>p. 185-186</3>

The Riot Games material shows rarefaction as policy. Legacy skins are presented as relatively rare because they are not always available in the store, and they reappear intermittently in bundles, promotions and events, amounting to scarcity by schedule, a device that converts time into price and access into rent. The Your Shop feature assembles offers by comparing the player's history with similar patterns, and the catalog becomes a variable showcase, built from inferences the consumer does not audit. The terms sustain this mobility by allowing the company, to the extent permitted by law, to modify or discontinue parts of the service and to remove or modify game content, including virtual products.

This rarefaction by governance appears in at least two modalities operationally adopted by Riot Games. A telling example lies in the so-called Legacy skins. They are presented as relatively rare not because of technical characteristics of the good, but because they “are not always available” in the store, reappearing intermittently in bundles, promotions and events <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025h)</2>.<3>p. 197-198</3>
Digital abundance, which would allow permanent availability, is reconfigured into “scarcity by schedule”, converting time into price and access into rent.<1>p. 198</1>

The official description itself states that the offers are produced by comparing the player's history with similar patterns, seeking to create offers that “you will like” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2023b)</2>.<3>p. 198</3>

Access to the catalog does not present itself to the user as a stable and knowable set of alternatives, but as a variable showcase, built from inferences that the consumer neither audits nor reconstructs.<1>p. 198</1>

The contract makes explicit that the service may be continuously updated and modified, and that the company may, to the extent permitted by law, “modify, suspend or discontinue” any part of the services, as well as “restrict your access to any feature or part of the Services” and “remove or modify Game Content, including Virtual Products” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 199</3>

None of this denies the product nature of what was bought. The IOC is a concretization of the immaterial product of Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC<1><2>2</2></1>, and the enjoyment of this product is subordinated to contractual and technological turnstiles, so that monetization comes to make up the functional substance of the object. Hence the criterion that matters to the lawyer, because the problem is not the mere existence of variations, but the possibility that changes in the architecture of enjoyment reorder, in an opaque way, the level of utility actually delivered.

If extraction depends on governing access, visibility and permanence, the “product” is not reduced to isolated content, but presents itself as an architecture of enjoyment and permissions that structures utility over time.<1>p. 208</1>

The IOC, as a concretization of the immaterial product in the sense of Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC<1><2>2</2></1>, appears here not as neutral content, but as a commodity form whose enjoyment is subordinated to contractual and technological turnstiles, so that one does not buy merely an item, but the revocable permission to remain within an ecosystem of signs.<3>p. 186</3>

Through the grammar of tolls, monetization strategies cease to be mere marketing accessories and come to make up the very functional substance of the Immaterial Object of Consumption (IOC).<1>p. 200-201</1>

In immaterial objects of consumption, utility is not exhausted in the act of acquisition, since it depends on continuous decisions of support, updating and continuity under the supplier's control <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52; p. 57)</2>. Therefore, the legal problem is not the mere existence of variations over time, but the possibility that changes in the architecture of enjoyment reorder, in an opaque way, the level of utility actually delivered.<3>p. 202-203</3>
Who sets the price when the currency belongs to the platform itself?

The demand monopoly has a consequence that legal language has barely explored, namely internal inflationary control. By defining the catalog, modulating scarcity and operating internal currencies, bundles and conversions, the supplier calibrates the general level of prices without the discipline of an open market, and inflation comes from governance by design, and not from material scarcity.

The ceiling ceases to be an impersonal market limit and becomes the consumer's behavioral tolerance as measured and tested by the supplier itself, in an environment in which exit is costly, external comparison is hindered and the auditability of the equivalence between expenditure and delivery is structurally reduced.<1>p. 176</1>
A direct offshoot of this demand monopoly, still little explored in traditional legal language, is the ecosystem's capacity for internal inflationary control.<1>p. 176</1>

By defining the catalog, modulating scarcity, managing windows of opportunity and operating internal currencies, bundles and conversions, the supplier comes to calibrate the general level of values charged, gradually raising price references and shifting anchors of acceptability without facing the discipline typical of markets with open supply and demand. Here, inflation does not stem from material scarcity, but from economic governance by design.<1>p. 176</1>

Price setting is not, in itself, condemnable. It is often legitimate when it stems from recognized innovation, consolidated reputation and real contestability, that is, the possibility of substitution and migration without prohibitive costs, and in material markets demand finds alternatives that work as a brake. On the platform, the supplier designs its own world of reference and exercises functions analogous to those of a market and to those of a normative authority, and the usurpation lies in occupying the position of price setter without the counterweights that legitimize it.

It must be recognized that certain agents may, often legitimately, act as price setters when their position stems from a verifiable combination of innovation recognized and protected within the limits of the system, consolidated reputation and competitive contestability, that is, the real possibility of substitution by competitors and of consumer migration without prohibitive costs.<1>p. 178</1>
In material markets, price setting tends to remain subject to external brakes because demand finds alternatives.<1>p. 178</1>

The supplier is not limited to competing within a market. It designs the very world of reference in which consumption takes place, controls catalog, visibility, rules of circulation, practical unit of account and conditions of permanence, and then comes to exercise, simultaneously, functions analogous to those of a market and to those of a normative authority, defining on its own the level of prices and the pace of internal inflation.<1>p. 179</1>

It is an appropriation of the position of price setter without the counterweights that legitimize it, since exit is costly, external comparison is artificially hindered (potentially made impossible) and the value of the object depends on parameters controlled unilaterally by the supplier itself.<1>p. 179</1>

Internal currencies are the point where the discussion meets the CDC. Proprietary currencies, bundles and bonuses work as a technology that removes the user from direct price comparison, with conversions and bundle sizes that can fragment the perception of spending, so that the balance tends to become a captive asset of the ecosystem. Price becomes a semiotic component of the offer, and signs of promotion and advantage may conceal conversion frictions, straining the duties of information, transparency and loyalty and, depending on the case, the prohibition of manifestly excessive advantage in Article 39, item V, of the CDC<1><2>3</2></1>. The silent personalization of offers, when anchored in the exploitation of urgency or fragility, may come close to the same prohibition, and open auditability and functional value equivalence are the parameters that make the distance between what is charged and what is delivered verifiable.

Internal units of value in closed digital ecosystems (points, proprietary “currencies”, bundles and bonuses) operate as a technology of economic governance of consumption by moving the user away from state currency and from direct price comparison toward unilaterally defined denominations, with conversion tables and bundle sizes that can fragment the perception of spending and induce successive top-ups (recurring leftovers, partial recharges, conditioned bonuses).<1>p. 207</1>

The relevant structural effect is economic lock-in: once converted into an internal unit, the balance tends to lose general fungibility and become a captive asset of the ecosystem, raising exit costs and making permanence a practical condition for not losing value already internalized.<1>p. 207</1>

At the dogmatic level, this requalifies price as a semiotic component of the offer: signs of “promotion”, “advantage” and “ease” may conceal conversion frictions, limits on circulation and restrictions on redemption, straining duties of information, transparency and loyalty and, depending on the case, the prohibition of manifestly excessive advantage (Article 39, item V, CDC<1><2>4</2></1>).<3>p. 207</3>

The decisive legal point is not the existence of transparent segmentations, but the silent differentiation that prevents the social comparability of price and hinders the evidentiary reconstruction of discrimination, since the criteria and data that sustain the modulation remain under the supplier's control. Seen this way, signs such as “personalization” may operate as an opaque technique of extraction, straining duties of material transparency and loyalty in the shaping of the offer and, when anchored in the exploitation of urgency or fragility, coming close to the logic of manifestly excessive advantage (Article 39, item V, CDC<1><2>4</2></1>). As internal control parameters, open auditability and functional value equivalence apply here to make the logic behind prices and terms verifiable, as well as to allow review of the dissociation between what is charged and what is delivered in IOCs.<3>p. 205</3>
What risk does the platform manufacture?

In a classic market, the relevant risk is that of defect, malfunction or breach of the offer. In continuous platform consumption, the most efficient risk is that of losing the window, the status and the opportunity, of falling behind and of seeing the symbolic identity built in the ecosystem depreciate. The platform calibrates this risk through temporal, offer, reward and sanctioning architectures, and coercion appears as functional and semiotic dependence built by design, and not as a prohibition or an order to buy.

In classic markets, relevant risk is the risk of defect, malfunction, insecurity, objective breach of the offer. Here, the efficient risk is another: the risk of missing the timing, of missing the window, of losing status, of “falling behind”, of seeing symbolic value evaporate and, of course, the risk of losing functional value within the ecosystem.<1>p. 210</1>

The decisive risk is the risk of losing opportunity, the risk of falling behind, the risk of not belonging, the risk of losing status, the risk of seeing the desired object go out of circulation and the risk of the symbolic identity built in the ecosystem suffering depreciation. This risk is not natural. It is calibrated by the platform through a temporal architecture, with seasons, splits, goals and missions. It is also calibrated by an offer architecture, with rotation, scheduled exclusions and variable catalogs. Added to this are a reward architecture, with progression and grind systems, and a sanctioning architecture, with bans, restrictions, automated penalties and opaque policies.<1>p. 211</1>
Coercion does not appear as violence, nor as direct prohibition, nor as an explicit imposition to buy; it appears as functional and semiotic dependence, built by design.<1>p. 210</1>

Missions show how time becomes currency. The command appears as an infantilized phrase of social contract, do something, get something, and turns time into currency without calling it labor. The contract incorporates the mechanism by saying that currency and virtual content may be obtained by purchase, by receipt or by earning, including through the completion of missions that the supplier itself defines and whose effectiveness depends on remaining in the ecosystem.

The command does not appear as an authoritarian order, but as an infantilized phrase of social contract: do something, get something. In terms of political economy, it is the typical gesture of turning time into currency without ever calling it labor, and of turning engagement into value without ever calling it production<1>p. 211</1>

The contract does not leave this mechanism at the level of the rhetoric of “events” and “fun”. It incorporates it into the very grammar of acquiring virtual goods by recording that access to Game Currency and Virtual Content may occur by purchase, by receipt or by earning, and that this “earning” may come from completing missions or tasks. The platform, therefore, formally recognizes that there is a path of acquisition that does not pass through direct payment, but through the completion of internal objectives, which are objectives defined by the supplier itself, with criteria and rewards defined by the supplier itself, and whose effectiveness depends on remaining in the ecosystem.<1>p. 212</1>

Three features of the toll tend to repeat. The coercive time window turns not acting into foreseeable loss, the sanction for absence makes the interruption of use trigger a downgrade of status, access or opportunity, and the opacity of price and equivalence, through intermediate currencies and conversions, prevents comparing cost and auditing promise and delivery. Combined, they make the toll coercion built into the mode of enjoyment. The battle pass is the recurring example, because the enjoyment of what was paid for depends on a race against time and a volume of engagement that, if not met, converts the payment into precarious access, and the same reasoning applies to rank decay for inactivity and to tiered currencies.

Three features tend to repeat. The first is the coercive time window, which shortens the space for decision and converts not acting into foreseeable loss. The second is the sanction for absence, in which the mere interruption of use triggers a downgrade of status, access or opportunity, turning permanence into a practical obligation. The third is the opacity of price and equivalence, obtained through intermediate currencies, bundles and conversions that prevent the consumer from comparing cost, measuring expenditure and auditing, in functional terms, the promise and the delivery. When these features combine, the toll ceases to be a simple marketing strategy and becomes coercion built into the mode of enjoyment.<1>p. 214-215</1>

A recurring example is the battle pass, in which the consumer pays for the possibility of unlocking items, but effective enjoyment depends on a race against time and an imposed volume of engagement that, if not met, converts the initial payment into precarious access and projected loss.<1>p. 215</1>

Another example is the programmed downgrade of ranking and visibility for inactivity, which converts absence into punishment and makes anxiety a cost of maintaining position, even when there is no new functional delivery that justifies the degradation.<1>p. 215</1>

A third example is the system of tiered virtual currencies, in which the purchase is not made in legal tender, but in intermediate credits and successive conversions that fragment perception, mask the real price and hinder comparison, reinforcing the inability to audit the equivalence between what is promised and what is delivered.<1>p. 215</1>

This set forms a metagame, in which the user competes to maintain access and status against the very structure of the environment, in a game unfair by design, because the supplier is at once referee, author of the rules, scorekeeper and beneficiary of the informational asymmetry. The legal relevance lies in the fact that these mechanisms reconfigure the consumer's decision-making autonomy and the adequacy of the object. The consumer decides under produced conditions, in a factual, semiotic and temporal vulnerability, and not only an informational one, which is the subject of the chapter on semiotic vulnerability.

The house always wins, not by rhetorical fatalism, but because the governance regime controls the conditions of victory, reconfigures goals, alters equivalences and manages scarcity, time and visibility as instruments of recurring extraction.<1>p. 216</1>

The platform treats the consumer relationship itself as a game in its own right, a metagame running parallel to the main product. The user is there for the matches, for interaction with others and for the competitive experience of the game, but, in the interface, is induced to take part in a continuous contest to maintain access, opportunity and status, now not against other players, but against the very structure that governs the environment. It is a game unfair by design, because the supplier is simultaneously referee, creator of the rules, scorekeeper and beneficiary of the informational asymmetry.<1>p. 215</1>

The legal relevance of these mechanisms stems from the fact that they reconfigure the consumer's decision-making autonomy and the very adequacy of the object, by shifting the center of value to conditions of enjoyment that are unstable, unilaterally managed and lacking in transparency.<1>p. 216</1>

The consumer decides under produced conditions. It is not only a matter of informational vulnerability. It is a matter of factual semiotic and temporal vulnerability, since the field of choice is pre-formatted and the economic meaning of the object depends on the very environment the supplier governs.<1>p. 216</1>
When does scarcity stop being a sales technique?

The dividing line lies in the way scarcity and temporality are mobilized to produce, predictably, frustration of utility, downgrading of adequacy or precarization of the value that grounded consent. When control over the existence and duration of the object is exercised systematically to intensify urgency and extraction, the discussion ceases to be about contractual freedom and becomes about purpose, because the rationality of the system reveals itself in the pattern, and not in the episode.

The dividing line does not lie in the fact that artificial scarcity exists, nor in the fact that the offer exploits rarity as a sales technique, but in the way scarcity and temporality are mobilized to produce, predictably, frustration of utility, downgrading of adequacy or precarization of the functional and positional value that grounded the consumer's consent.<1>p. 213</1>

When this control over the existence and duration of the object is exercised systematically to intensify urgency, dependence and extraction, the problem ceases to be merely “contractual freedom” or “legitimate business model” and becomes one of purpose. The rationality of the system reveals itself in the pattern, not in the episode.<1>p. 212-213</1>

Hence the distinction between positional scarcity and corrosive scarcity. Selling a commemorative edition or a rare cosmetic for a short window may manufacture urgency, provided it keeps the due delivery intact and gives clear parameters on duration, form of access, limits of the offer and any future repetition, and this additive rarity acts on choice without downgrading what has already been acquired. Scarcity is corrosive when what has already been obtained deliberately loses status, power or use value if the consumer does not pay for new layers or does not comply with retention routines, which amounts to nonperformance manufactured by architecture, because maintaining value becomes a toll charged in money or in compulsory presence.

This distinction can be visualized through the contrast between positional scarcity and corrosive scarcity. The sale of a commemorative edition or of a rare cosmetic item for a short window may manufacture urgency and capture value through opportunity, provided it keeps the due delivery intact and offers the consumer clear parameters on duration, form of access, limits of the offer and any future repetition. It is additive rarity, whose effect falls on the consumer's choice without downgrading the integrity of what has already been acquired nor degrading the experience of those who choose not to buy.<1>p. 213</1>

A different matter is the design in which the object or the set of advantages already obtained deliberately lose status, power, practical relevance or use value if the consumer does not pay for new layers, does not comply with retention routines or does not submit to imposed update cycles, manufacturing nonperformance by architecture. In this second scenario, scarcity ceases to be a simple commercial strategy and comes to operate as a mechanism of frustration of adequacy, because maintaining the functional value of the object is converted into a permanent toll, charged in money or in compulsory presence, which reconfigures the contract as a dynamic of unstable permission and reinforces, through the very structure of the design, the supplier's governance asymmetry.<1>p. 213</1>

At the legal level, artificial scarcity is usually anchored in exclusivity rights, revocable licenses, non-transferability and reservations of the right to change, which give the supplier the power to define what exists, for how long and under which narratives, including as to positional attributes sold as part of the price. That is why it forms part of an architectural teleology, and it is at this threshold that it becomes relevant to qualifying the deviation of purpose, when the equivalence between promise and delivery is made opaque or deliberately frustrated.

Artificial scarcity thus works as an economic operator and as a legal operator. At the economic level, it converts replicable goods into assets apt to sustain recurring monetization. At the legal level, it is often anchored in exclusivity rights and in contractual arrangements that authorize unilateral control of the catalog, the rules and the very ontological status of the object, such as revocable licenses, non-transferability and reservations of the right to change, as well as access and interface architectures that make enjoyment an unstable permission.<1>p. 214</1>

The result is a form of market in which asymmetry is not limited to the supplier's “better knowledge”. It materializes in the supplier's very capacity to define what exists, for how long it exists, under what conditions it exists and under which narratives it exists, including as to positional attributes offered as components of the price. Therefore, artificial scarcity must be understood as part of an architectural teleology. It forms part of a set of design choices oriented toward extraction and not toward the simple efficient organization of a naturally limited resource, and it is at this threshold that it ceases to be merely a commercial strategy and becomes a legally relevant category for qualifying the deviation of purpose when the equivalence between promise and delivery is made opaque or deliberately frustrated.<1>p. 214</1>
What can a buyer claim when an item sold as exclusive comes back cheaper?

One scenario depends neither on loss of access nor on extreme degradation of functionality, and that is why it is the most common. When the platform sells an item at a high price under a promise of exclusivity, or presents exclusivity as an attribute that justifies the price, it makes that quality part of the content of the offer, and the consumer also pays for the promised rarity, for the status and for the social distinction the ecosystem enforces. When that promise does not hold, there is positional deception by omission.

There is, however, an even more common mode, just as abusive, that depends neither on loss of access nor on extreme degradation of functionality, and that manifests itself as positional deception by omission. When the platform sells an item at a high price under the promise of exclusivity, or presents exclusivity as a relevant attribute to justify price and expenditure, it incorporates that quality into the content of the offer and into the perceived utility of the object. In these cases, the consumer does not pay only for aesthetics or immediate availability, but for the promised rarity, for the status and for the social distinction that the ecosystem's own symbolic architecture enforces.<1>p. 213-214</1>

The scenario has two elements, and both need to be demonstrated. The first is the reappearance of the same item, after some time, in an alternative store, in a special currency, in an aggressive promotion or at a significantly lower price. The second is that the temporal limitation of exclusivity was not adequately and comprehensibly disclosed at the time of purchase. When both are present, there is a retroactive reconfiguration of the value delivered and a breach of transparency, with potential classification as misleading advertising by omission and as breach of the offer, as well as a rupture of the equivalence between what was spent and the legitimately expected utility.

Scarcity, here, may operate as a device for capturing consent under informational inadequacy, with potential classification as misleading advertising by omission and breach of the offer, besides breaking the equivalence between expenditure and utility delivered as legitimately expected.<1>p. 214</1>

The legal consequence is explicit, and it is framed in terms of what may follow. A later change to the attribute that justified the price may call for material restoration through the typical consumer remedies, which are refund, price reduction or equivalent functional compensation, and it may also open room for damages, provided that additional harm arising from the deception is shown. None of these remedies is automatic, and equivalent functional compensation is measured by the criteria of the chapter on functional value equivalence.

No particular item is classified in advance, and the scenario should not be applied without both elements. The material on Legacy skins shows where the analysis begins, because official support describes their rarity as planned unavailability and states that they may reappear from time to time in bundles or promotions. The decisive question is what the offer said, at the time of purchase, about duration, form of access, limits and future repetition. Reconstructing that offer is the subject of the chapter on proof.

In the official support material, the rarity of Legacy skins is described as the direct result of planned unavailability, and not as a natural trait of the good. The page states directly that “Legacy skins are relatively rare because they are not always available for purchase in the Store” and adds that, “from time to time”, they can be found “in bundles or in promotions during events” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025h)</2>.<3>p. 198</3>

The sale of a commemorative edition or of a rare cosmetic item for a short window may manufacture urgency and capture value through opportunity, provided it keeps the due delivery intact and offers the consumer clear parameters on duration, form of access, limits of the offer and any future repetition.<1>p. 213</1>
Is the consumer only a consumer?

The consumer also hands over what is not money. Continuous extraction depends on a return of value that comes in the form of activity, and each session, match, purchase or abandonment feeds metrics and engagement cycles. The Public Beta Environment, which official support describes as a server for testing upcoming features and eliminating bugs before launch, makes this visible, as does the clause that allows the company to freely use, without payment, the suggestions sent by the user, and the one that restricts use to personal and non-commercial purposes, leaving content creators in a zone of conditioned tolerance.

Continuous extraction is not sustained only by recurring charges, since it depends on a return of value that does not come in the form of price, but in the form of activity. Each session, click, match, search, comment, purchase, abandonment, return and comparison keeps the ecosystem alive and feeds metrics, network effects, reputations, hierarchies and engagement cycles.<1>p. 217</1>

In official support, the PBE is described as a server on which one can “test upcoming features” and which allows the company to “eliminate any bugs” found “before it is implemented in the game environment” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024j)</2>.<3>p. 218</3>

In Clause 6.1, the contract states that “We value your feedback”, but prohibits sending it and, if sent, provides that the company may “freely use” the ideas and do so “without any payment to you” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 218</3>

On the one hand, the contract insists that use is “personal” and “non-commercial”, pushing creative work into a zone of conditioned tolerance, dependent on authorization, exceptions or a specific program.<1>p. 219</1>

The example of greatest interest for the duty to inform is the preview. Until the research was concluded, the client, which is the program through which the user accesses the service, offered no robust mechanism in the purchase flow for getting to know the experience of a skin before buying it, and company representatives publicly acknowledged that users often do not know precisely what they are acquiring. External skin showcase channels thus work as prostheses of the duty of information, performing a necessary function without corresponding legal status.

As of the date of conclusion of this research, the client does not offer, in the purchase flow itself, a robust and generalized preview mechanism that allows the user to audit the experience of a skin before acquiring it, so that the decision depends, to a relevant extent, on external mediations that display, compare and describe the content.<1>p. 219-220</1>

Riot's own representatives publicly acknowledge this discomfort when announcing experiments with mechanisms for offering skin previews, making explicit that the user often does not know precisely what they are acquiring at the time of purchase<1>p. 220</1>

In this void, channels such as SkinSpotlights come to function, in practice, as prostheses of the ecosystem's duty of information, because they display what the consumer cannot audit within the normal purchase circuit<1>p. 220</1>

The result is that a formally external agent is incorporated as a necessary piece of the circulation apparatus, delivering intelligibility, reducing the risk of regret and sustaining the consumer's practical confidence in the purchase, without receiving any legal status corresponding to the economic function it performs within the regime.<1>p. 220</1>

To name this position, Karl Marx's figure of the lumpenproletariat enters by strict structural homology and without exegetical pretension, and the consumer appears as an incorporated exterior. No labor categories are transposed and no employment relationship is asserted, and this fact does not change the nature of the relationship, which remains one of consumption. It qualifies the governance asymmetry and reinforces the duties of material transparency, loyalty and protection of trust in continuous adhesion contracts. Extending the incorporated exterior to other intermediation platforms is a hypothesis still to be tested.

At this point, with a strictly functional scope and without pretension of exegetical reconstruction, it is justified to mobilize, by strict structural homology, the figure of the lumpenproletariat as presented by Karl Marx. The aim is not to transpose categories of the employment relationship to digital consumption, nor to shift the framing of the consumer microsystem to a general theory of class struggle.<1>p. 221</1>

It is not a matter of asserting an employment relationship, but of identifying an unpaid social co-production of value, captured and converted into revenue through unilateral governance of the rules, of visibility, of the catalog and of the conditions of enjoyment. In dogmatic terms, this fact does not change the nature of the relationship as consumption. It qualifies the governance asymmetry and reinforces the centrality of duties of material transparency, loyalty and protection of trust in continuous adhesion contracts, precisely because the supplier manages, without real auditability by the consumer, the parameters that define what is worth something, what appears and what is considered “rare”.<1>p. 221-222</1>

It is recorded, as a hypothesis of extension to be tested in later works, that the notion of “incorporated exterior” does not depend on the specific domain analyzed here, but describes a recurring structural position in intermediation platforms and in private governance by architecture.<1>p. 226</1>

Two features complete the figure.
