The consumer pays for equipment, energy and connectivity to remain in an environment that converts their presence into someone else's asset, and receives badges, skins and prestige levels that work as a payment that does not remunerate, only regulates. The effect is identity captivity, an institutional and semiotic dependence, and not a psychological one in the individualizing sense, in which leaving costs recognition, reputation and continuity of trajectory. The relevance of the concept is not to create a new good, but to bring under control a specific form of loss, in which the integrity of agency and symbolic identity are corroded by instability, opacity and manufactured risk.

In the regime of IOCs, the consumer comes to finance, with their own resources, the minimum infrastructure of their own economic and semiotic incorporation, paying for hardware, electricity and connectivity in order to remain in an environment that converts their presence into someone else's asset.<1>p. 223</1>

Badges, skins, emblems, passes, prestige levels and signs of distinction work as payment, but a payment that does not remunerate, only regulates. The supplier trades lines of code and calibrated scarcity for hours of the consumer's life, attention and behavioral predictability, producing the cheapest form of bribe yet observable in markets, since what is granted to the user has no intrinsic value independent of the ecosystem.<1>p. 224</1>

The fear of losing what has been accumulated, of seeing one's digital identity devalued or erased, becomes an instrument of discipline, consolidating a form of existential captivity that adds to the economic captivity already described. This effect can be named, with operational precision, as identity captivity, understood as a modality of dependence in which the exit cost is not reduced to the patrimonial level, but involves loss of recognition, of reputation and of narrative continuity objectified in public performance records, collections, histories and signs of distinction produced within the ecosystem. Dependence, in this register, is not psychological in the individualizing sense, but institutional and semiotic, because it stems from a regime of visibility and sanction that defines what counts as value, belonging and legitimate progress and, correlatively, defines how this can be downgraded, erased or disauthorized.<1>p. 224-225</1>
What does the business model reveal about the purpose of the design?

The model that results from these readings can be described as a teleological architecture of continuous extraction, which shifts economic command from the product to the conditions of access, permanence and circulation and rests on three integrated operators. Artificial scarcity reinserts rarity where technique would tend toward abundance and describes the access regime, and not the object. Manufactured risk converts this regime into a discipline of presence, and consumption ceases to be an event and becomes a routine. Diffuse productivity closes the circuit, because the user's activity becomes data, social proof and network effect, and the user takes part in the valorization of the environment that governs them.

Digital platforms can be understood as teleological architectures of continuous extraction, institutional and technical-functional designs aimed at stabilizing rent and power in markets of immaterial goods, shifting economic command from the product to the conditions of access, permanence and circulation.<1>p. 243</1>

It is from this convergence that the business model of platforms can be described as an architecture of continuous extraction applied to ontologically non-scarce goods. Its stability depends on three structural operators acting in an integrated way: production of artificial scarcity, manufacture of risk as a discipline of presence and capture of the user's diffuse productivity as an economic and semiotic input.<1>p. 244</1>
Scarcity, here, does not describe the object, since it describes the access regime, being a mode of governing circulation.<1>p. 245</1>

By organizing the experience as a continuous management of the possibility of loss, an environment is created in which permanence ceases to be an episodic option and comes to operate as rational conduct protecting investments and position, so that consumption ceases to be an event and comes to function as routine.<1>p. 246</1>

The user's activity sustains the ecosystem and is converted into assets, into data and metrics, social proof and diffusion, symbolic validation, network effects, standards of comparison and hierarchies of visibility. In this arrangement, the user is not merely the recipient of an offer, because they take a material part in increasing the value of the environment that governs them.<1>p. 246</1>

Competition becomes a contest between ecosystems, and whoever wins it imposes conditions of access, permanence and visibility, while switching costs, network effects and accumulated investments form a captive demand. The rework that redesigns a character, its effects and its place in the competitive contest shows the consequence, because it devalues past investments without any equivalence mechanism and without letting consumers take with them what they acquired. While reputation, history and acquired goods remain trapped in the same enclosure, leaving is formally possible but economically irrational.

When the platform holds the infrastructure of circulation and the grammar of symbolic value (by defining what counts as rarity, what counts as status, what counts as a goal and what counts as belonging), it turns competition into a contest between ecosystems and over governance capacity, and not between isolated products. Whoever wins the contest for an ecosystem comes to hold not only market share, but the power to impose conditions of access, permanence and visibility, reorganizing behavior at scale and converting private rules into competitive advantage. This feeds back into a captivity of demand: switching costs, functional and symbolic dependencies, network externalities and accumulated investments make exit costly and permanence structurally probable.<1>p. 245</1>

The rework that redesigns a character, effects and position in the metagame is functionally equivalent to a reordering of the territory that devalues past investments without offering an internal mechanism of value equivalence, and without allowing the consumer to take what they acquired outside the platform's jurisdiction. The contemporary fief is sustained precisely by this asymmetry, since exit is formally possible, but economically irrational when reputation, history, ties, signs of distinction and acquired goods remain trapped in the same technical enclosure.<1>p. 247</1>

The legal question shifts. The diagnosis does not depend on attributing the phenomenon to compulsive consumption or bad choices, because the relevant coercion is dependence produced by design. Three mechanisms recur, the unilateral modulation of the conditions of enjoyment, functional opacities and the continuous calibration of behavior through A/B tests, which compare versions of the service across groups of users, through gamification and through selective frictions. Under these conditions, the question is no longer merely contractual and becomes one of the legitimacy of the architecture, that is, of the economic purpose built into the normal functioning of the service.

The question then objectively detaches itself from the moral aspect and becomes legal-structural. The diagnosis does not depend on attributing the phenomenon to “compulsive consumption” or “bad choices”, because the relevant coercion does not present itself as an explicit imposition to buy, but as dependence produced by design, by governance and by narratives that organize value and belonging within a closed circuit.<1>p. 246</1>

The economic architecture of the platform contains a teleology of continuous extraction that materializes in recurring mechanisms. Among them is the unilateral modulation of the conditions of enjoyment, with changes to rules, prices, access levels, ranking criteria and recommendation regimes. Also present are functional opacities that prevent verification and challenge, such as non-auditable criteria, informational asymmetries and uncertainty about what determines outcomes. Finally, there is the continuous calibration of behavior, through A/B tests, gamification and selective frictions that make certain paths natural and others costly.<1>p. 246</1>

When the consumer is kept as a serf of the infrastructure through artificial scarcity and manufactured risk, the legal question ceases to be merely contractual and becomes one of the legitimacy of the architecture, that is, of the economic purpose built into the normal mode of functioning of the service.<1>p. 246-247</1>

Two operations must be kept apart. Architectural teleology describes the economic purpose materialized as design aimed at retention and continuous capture, and reclassifying digital businesses as architectures of extraction provides a theoretical basis for questioning whether the purposes embedded in the design may be unlawful. Qualification as an unlawful act of abusive teleology comes only where appropriate, and it rests on the permanence of the mechanism, not on an episodic reading of a single term or on a snapshot of a patch, which is the game's update package.
The consequence is that the economic purpose of the model materializes as institutional design, that is, as architectural teleology oriented toward retention and continuous capture.<1>p. 231-232</1>

Articulated together, the three dimensions make it possible to reclassify digitally based businesses as architectures of continuous value extraction, operating on functionally defined immaterial goods. It is a reclassification that provides a theoretical basis for questioning the potential unlawfulness of the intentions and purposes embedded in the design of platforms.<1>p. 143-144</1>

If the ecosystem is structured to produce risk, scarcity and dependence as engines of consumption, legal analysis cannot remain restricted to the episodic reading of a term nor to a snapshot of a patch. What is qualified is a regime of governed enjoyment. It is this permanence of the mechanism that makes it possible to move from economic description to the identification of an operative purpose and, when appropriate, to the characterization of the unlawful act of abusive teleology.<1>p. 216-217</1>

The requirements of this qualification belong to the chapter on abusive teleology, which rests on the purpose objectively inscribed in the arrangement and dispenses with proof of psychological intent, so that to speak of the intentions and purposes of the design is to speak of the design, and not of anyone's will. The economic description prepares the attribution of liability without replacing it, and already points to the direction of protection, which must bear on integrity, restoration and controllability, all the more so the closer the platform comes to practical sovereignty over what was acquired.

The closer the platform comes to practical sovereignty over access, visibility and the meaning of what was acquired, the more the axis of protection needs to fall on integrity, restoration and controllability, and not on a narrow notion of one-off delivery.<1>p. 247</1>

The category does not depend on imputing subjective psychological intent nor on locating a single act as sufficient cause, because its object is the architectural program as a set of repeated choices that organizes possibilities, introduces frictions, manages visibilities, distributes sanctions and stabilizes dependencies in the performance of the relationship.<1>p. 448</1>

The focus is on the functional purpose objectively inscribed in the arrangement, as revealed by its replicability, by its internal coherence and by its repeated impact on the consumer's experience.<1>p. 732</1>
Why are visibility and recognition part of the good?

If extraction depends on permanence, the platform needs to govern attention and meaning, and its power lies in defining what is seen, what is comparable and what is desirable. The attention economy is no longer a metaphor, because the decisive scarce resource becomes the user's exposure time, and not the technical availability of the good.
Economics and semiotics cease to be parallel layers, because regulating perception, comparison and visibility is regulating the decision field itself.<1>p. 248</1>

If extraction under platforms depends on permanence and on governance of access, it needs to govern the field in which this permanence is decided in practice, that of attention and signification.<1>p. 248</1>

Power is not limited to charging or prohibiting, since it is realized by defining what is seen, what is comparable, what is desirable and what gains social traction, pushing certain alternatives toward “naturalness” and others toward practical invisibility.<1>p. 248</1>
Along the same line, “attention economy” ceases to be a metaphor. The decisive scarce resource is not the technical availability of the good, but the user's exposure time.<1>p. 249</1>

The anthropology of consumption provides analytical support for describing this governance. Mary Douglas and Baron Isherwood treat goods as an infrastructure of classification, which provides marking services and stabilizes boundaries of belonging, so the cost of leaving is not only a loss of property but a risk of isolation. Arjun Appadurai treats value as a situated judgment, within regimes and a politics of value, so that managing the catalog, rarity and visibility is managing the practical conditions of value itself.
The anthropology of consumption will enter, along this path, as analytical support for understanding how the visible and the desirable also become economically governed dimensions.<1>p. 145</1>

Goods stabilize hierarchies, boundaries of belonging and the intelligibility of the social world by providing marking services capable of organizing calendars, appraising relationships and sustaining reciprocities <1>Isherwood</1><2>(Douglas; Isherwood, 1996, p. xxii; p. 40-41)</2>. From this perspective, the relevance lies in offering a vocabulary to describe the immaterial object of consumption as something whose social utility depends on social legibility and belonging within a managed ecosystem, which makes it possible to read the exit cost not only as patrimonial loss, but as a risk of isolation and weakening of ties.<3>p. 248-249</3>

The consequence is that the relevant question ceases to be “how much does it cost” and becomes “which frames make something appear as desirable, comparable and rare”, because value is not inherent in the object, but a judgment produced by subjects and endorsed by a real or imagined exchange <1>Appadurai</1><2>(Appadurai, 1986, p. 3-4)</2>. For this reason, the author prefers to speak of regimes of value, whose coherence may vary according to the situation and the commodity, without requiring full cultural consensus to operate <3>Appadurai</3><4>(Appadurai, 1986, p. 14-15)</4>.<5>p. 250</5>
The notion of “politics of value” makes explicit the field of power that sustains these regimes.<1>p. 251</1>

Igor Kopytoff describes the cultural biography of objects, classified and reclassified over time. On platforms, retiring items from the catalog, changing their rarity and repositioning them around events are singularization managed by the platform, which keeps nominal ownership in place while reordering the item's cultural biography. Grant McCracken shows that part of meaning is perishable and requires renewal, and daily logins, missions, events, seasons and passes can be read as the ritualization of this renewal, which turns into a discipline of presence.

The discussion gains an additional tool for describing mutations of value over time without resorting to morality or psychology. In this sense, the perspective of culturally informed economic biography treats the object as a culturally constructed entity, endowed with specific meanings and classified and reclassified into socially constituted categories <1>Kopytoff</1><2>(Kopytoff, 1986, p. 68)</2>.<3>p. 252-253</3>
In platform ecosystems, routines such as daily login, missions, limited-time events, seasons and passes can be read as operationalized ritualization.<1>p. 255</1>

Updating one's repertoire becomes a discipline of presence, and the discipline of presence sustains the toll by converting the renewal of signs into a practical obligation to show up under managed visibility.<1>p. 257</1>

The IOC thus behaves as a functional and semiotic bundle, and governing signs and regimes of appearance means governing the object itself. Validation by consensus, the discipline of presence and an exit cost enlarged by lost reputation and belonging convert technical abundance into socially perceived scarcity. The result is an identity captivity in which the toll works as a fee for keeping one's place. The promise of the good therefore includes expectations of social utility that depend on visibility and collective validation.

The IOC does not behave as a “good” only because of an isolated functional utility, but as a functional and semiotic bundle, in which enjoyment depends on operations of public legibility and collective recognition. Thus, governing signs, regimes of appearance and collective recognition is not a gesture external to supply, but a way of governing the object itself and its utility over time, because it is in this field that what “counts” as relevant difference, socially perceived rarity and belonging is formed.<1>p. 252</1>

The conversion of technical abundance into socially perceived scarcity is anchored in three coupled mechanisms. First, by validation by consensus, in which metrics, display and circulation produce performed recognition and make value “seem” natural. Second, by a discipline of presence, in which the perishability of meaning and the timing of enjoyment turn updating one's repertoire into a practical obligation to show up. And third, by an exit cost enlarged by reputational losses and losses of belonging, so that the act of abandoning the ecosystem does not merely imply losing utility, but losing social legibility and recognizable position. The result is an identity captivity, in which the toll stabilizes as a fee for keeping one's place, not as a one-off price of an item.<1>p. 258</1>
The promise of the good includes expectations of social utility that depend on public visibility and collective validation in the ecosystem.<1>p. 258</1>

Hence the claim that matters most in litigation, that unilateral changes to the criteria of display, circulation, rarity and comparison bear on the semiotic core of the object's utility. This does not make it unlawful to ritualize or update signs, and qualification as abusive teleology is reserved for cases in which these arrangements are no longer ordinary management of the service. How the symbolic dimension enters the comparison between what was promised and what was delivered is the subject of the chapter on functional value equivalence.

Unilateral changes that reconfigure criteria of display, circulation, rarity and grammars of comparison are not neutral “cosmetics”, since they bear on the semiotic core that makes up the social utility of the IOC and structures the consumer's decision.<1>p. 258</1>

It remains to advance, with greater granularity, to the concrete operations of interface, curation and circulation through which the platform produces meaning and a discipline of presence, and to the legal qualification of these arrangements when they cease to be ordinary management of the service and come to constitute abusive teleology, by reordering promise, enjoyment and the minimum preservation of the value legitimately expected over time.<1>p. 258-259</1>
Can't the consumer simply leave?

The first objection is that consumers can leave whenever they want. The answer, with Varoufakis, is that a demand monopoly need not prohibit competitors, because it is enough to make migration costly, so that the formal freedom to leave exists while the material freedom becomes far more expensive. Leaving means abandoning history, reputation, items, progression and social networks, and the more the object is governed enjoyment, the more competition becomes a contest over lock-in rather than over the excellence of the good.

The demand monopoly stabilizes itself through switching costs and material barriers to exit, since there is no need to prohibit competitors. It is enough to make migration costly by holding collections and ties hostage, so that the formal freedom to leave exists, but the material freedom becomes severely more expensive.<1>p. 175-176</1>

Power is stabilized not only by price, but by exit cost. Leaving means abandoning history, reputation, library, items, progression, emotional investments, social networks and, in certain cases, the very capacity to take part in communities that organize themselves within that ecosystem. The more the object of consumption is governed enjoyment rather than a delivered thing, the more the dependence is on infrastructure, and the more “competition” becomes a contest for lock-in by design, not for the excellence of the good.<1>p. 217</1>

The second is that technofeudalism is a mere metaphor or an ideological import. With Varoufakis, the feudal grammar describes material dependence mediated by infrastructure and access, and the feudal logic is not a medievalizing aesthetic but an economic organization in which the platform holds the infrastructure and the power to rewrite the conditions under which consumption gains value.

The choice of the feudal grammar does not function as a decorative metaphor, but as a description of material dependence mediated by infrastructure and access <1>Varoufakis</1><2>(Varoufakis, 2024, p. 78-80)</2>.<3>p. 151</3>

The feudal logic, in this sense, does not describe a medievalizing aesthetic, but a form of economic organization in which the platform holds the monopoly of infrastructure and the power to rewrite, over time, the material conditions of valorization and existence of consumption.<1>p. 243</1>

The third is that the change is simply the service evolving, and the frustration mere subjective displeasure. But, with Dowbor, when utility depends on recognition and visibility governed by the supplier, unilateral changes are not background noise but an instrument of capture. And, with Douglas and Isherwood, being left out of the system of social marking means a risk of practical silencing and of fewer future options. The limit lies in the criterion already set, which reaches redesign without sufficient transparency between offer and delivery, and not variation as such.

Dowbor's interpretive key matters here because it reconstructs, at the micro level, what is often naturalized as an update routine or mere “evolution of the service”. In platform ecosystems, the utility of the immaterial good depends on recognition, visibility and permanence governed by the supplier itself, so that unilateral changes are not background noise, but an instrument of capture.<1>p. 184</1>

Being left outside the reach of this system is not a subjective discomfort. It is a risk of practical silencing, of a reduced voice and fewer future options, with a direct impact on the very rationality of choice <1>Isherwood</1><2>(Douglas; Isherwood, 1996, p. 63-65)</2>.<3>p. 251</3>

When the redesign of the immaterial object occurs without sufficient transparency for the consumer to understand, at least in material terms, the correspondence between what is presented in the offer and what is actually delivered, the change ceases to be perceived as a simple adjustment and comes to operate as an opacifying governance of enjoyment.<1>p. 203</1>
Does every digital product depend on governance?

The economic reading does not claim that every digital product depends on continuous governance, and even about the game it says only that it tends to require it, as a complex audiovisual experience made up of multiple intellectual goods and related services. Nor does it deny that the productive base persists, and what it takes from Dowbor is the subordination of that base to informational and financial command.

The very object delivered by the interactive entertainment industry already tends to require this continuous governance, since the game is configured as a complex audiovisual experience and as an organized compound of multiple intellectual goods and related services, exploited through an equally complex contractual network.<1>p. 156</1>

The decisive point for the present analysis is not to deny the persistence of the productive base, but to show its structural subordination to informational-financial command, which comes to define who accesses the market, through which mediations and under which conditions of subjection <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 3; p. 27)</2>.<3>p. 188</3>

Varoufakis's proposals, from technodemocracy to an architecture of digital rights, are his own, and they do not serve as a legal solution. What matters is less the strategy for overcoming technofeudalism than the insight that the infrastructure that organizes enjoyment also organizes the difficulty of collective challenge. With Dowbor, who refuses to see this closure as fate, regulation operates as a design of continuity, quality, auditability and material transparency, a problem that can be framed in the language of the CDC.

In conclusion, Varoufakis frames the “escape” from technofeudalism not as an incremental package of regulatory corrections, but as a change of regime. A passage to “another reality” (which he also names technodemocracy), founded on the socialization of the decisive instruments of production, distribution, collaboration and communication.<1>p. 181</1>
At the strictly digital level, Varoufakis proposes an architecture of digital rights and remuneration to replace the “deception” of free services.<1>p. 182</1>

For this thesis, the point is less the political strategy for overcoming technofeudalism and more the perception that the infrastructure that organizes access and enjoyment also organizes isolation, comparison, dispersion and the difficulty of collective challenge.<1>p. 165</1>
At the same time, Dowbor refuses to treat this systemic closure as an unavoidable technological fatality.<1>p. 204</1>

The decisive point, therefore, is not “technology”, but the legal-institutional vector that structures access and defines whether technical abundance is converted into inclusion or into toll. That is why regulation is not reduced to an ex post patch; in network powers and infrastructural positions, it operates as a structural design of continuity, quality, auditability and material transparency. In this scope, the problem can be formulated in consumer-law language (CDC), above all with regard to the material shaping of the offer and of enjoyment in governed ecosystems.<1>p. 203</1>

Nor does the reference to the right of sculptors and visual artists to share in resale gains transplant that institution. It only shows that concentrating all the gains of collective symbolic chains in one hand is not a legal inevitability, a question of the social function of intellectual property that the chapter on intellectual property takes up again.

The right to share in resale gains, granted to sculptors and visual artists, exemplifies a mechanism by which the creator retains a limited share in the later economic fruits of their work. The reference does not aim to automatically transplant the institution, but to indicate that the full concentration of gains derived from collectively fed symbolic chains is not a legal inevitability. In attention ecosystems, the social function of intellectual property requires at least that the question be raised again about the limits of the full appropriation of value by a single entity when the economic chain depends structurally on authors, artists, communities and consumers.<1>p. 144</1>

What remains is the question of how far the Law can limit models that turn access into dependence and enjoyment into a toll circuit, which shifts the inquiry from the clause and the episode to the economic purpose built into the arrangement.

The question that arises, therefore, is to what extent the Law can impose limits on business models that, in order to monetize the immaterial, need to turn access into dependence, promise into a permanent cycle and enjoyment into a toll circuit. The problem shifts from the atomized examination of events and clauses to the evaluation of the economic purpose built into the arrangement, that is, to the examination of an institutional design that produces continuous extraction as a normal result of its functioning.<1>p. 247</1>
